TEXT: What would the world's largest cities be like if the landmasses were rotated by 90 degrees?
Some get colder.
Mexico City high in the polar mountains is buried beneath nice sheep.
Jakarta is the new svalbard, a desolate coastal rock too far north for even most Norwegian's.
Polkata and deli are ice-bound, sealed off from the warmer world by the Himalayas.
Hong Kong, Manila, Karachi, and Mumbai are similar to our world's anchorage or rakey of it.
The ocean isn't frozen solid, but it sure is cold.
Many cities remain comfortably habitable, albeit with some changes.
Seoul, Osaka, Tokyo, Shanghai, and New York City are among the least affected cities,
with climates roughly similar to their previous ones.
Shanghai does get colder, but seasonal extremes in all five cities get milder, particularly in Seoul,
and substantially wetter.
Cairo has moved slightly south.
It's now surrounded by coastal savannah with spots of rainforest found around the mouth of the Nile.
So Paulo and Buenos Aires cool down a little bit.
Their climate is somewhere between that of our old New England and that of our old regular England.
Los Angeles is cool and mild.
The steady sea breeze carrying moisture up into the San Gabriel Mountains makes LA one of the
raniest places in the new US.
It closely resembles a wetter version of our Seattle.
And a few cities get much hotter.
Moscow is extremely hot and very dry with a climate somewhere between our fenix and our bagged
head.
And London sits in a steamy jungle with a climate generally resembling Bangkok's.
Spicy curry is now climatically appropriate, the tems is full of piranha, and it's the only place on
earth where tigers apologize as they attack you.
